sections.section_title: The Setting: Mountain, Posture, and Audience
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage establishes the setting for Jesus's authoritative teaching: ascending a mountain (recalling Moses on Sinai), sitting down (the posture of an authoritative teacher), with the discourse directed primarily to disciples but overheard by the crowds.

The neutral reading finds this passage identifies who stands in divine favor as the kingdom arrives -- the poor in spirit, mourning, meek, those hungering for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, peacemakers, and persecuted -- with the kingdom belonging to them as a present reality, and persecution for Jesus's sake placing the disciples in the prophetic succession.

sections.section_title: Salt and Light: The Function of the Disciples
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage assigns the disciples a preserving (salt) and illuminating (light) function in the world, with an explicit warning that salt can lose its distinctive character and be thrown out, and that the disciples' role is not automatically preserved.
sections.relevance: The salt metaphor directly warns that the disciples' distinctive identity can be lost: 'If salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out.' The neutral reading interprets this as a warning that the disciples' kingdom identity must be maintained and that they 'are not automatically preserved in their role.' This bears on the permanence question because it describes a scenario in which those who are currently functioning as kingdom people lose that function irreversibly and are discarded. The word for 'lost its taste' (moranthe) connects to the 'foolish' man of 7:26 and the 'foolish' virgins of 25:2-3, reinforcing the link between loss of character and ultimate rejection.
key_phrases: if salt has lost its taste
how shall its saltiness be restored
no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet

sections.section_title: Jesus and the Torah: Fulfillment, Not Abolition
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage is the interpretive key to the entire discourse, declaring that Jesus came not to abolish but to fulfill the Torah and Prophets, and establishing that entrance into the kingdom requires a righteousness exceeding that of the scribes and Pharisees.
sections.relevance: The statement 'unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven' makes kingdom entry explicitly conditional on a quality of conduct. This is addressed to those already following Jesus, implying that following him does not automatically guarantee kingdom entry -- a specific standard of lived righteousness is required. The passage functions as the thesis for the entire discourse that follows, establishing conduct as the criterion for kingdom participation.
key_phrases: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees
you will never enter the kingdom of heaven
whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage extends the Torah's prohibition of murder to the inner disposition of anger and contempt, warning of escalating consequences -- judgment, the council, and the gehenna of fire -- for hostility toward a brother within the community.
sections.relevance: The warning that anger and contempt toward a brother make one 'liable to the gehenna of fire' implies that those within the believing community face the possibility of ultimate destruction based on their conduct toward others. The urgency of reconciliation ('you will never get out until you have paid the last penny') suggests consequences that are severe and difficult to reverse, indicating that ongoing conduct within the community of disciples directly affects one's ultimate standing.
key_phrases: everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment
whoever says 'You fool!' shall be liable to the gehenna of fire
you will never get out until you have paid the last penny

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage extends the Torah's prohibition of adultery to the internal disposition of lust, using hyperbolic language about self-mutilation to emphasize that no cost is too high to avoid the destruction of the whole self in gehenna.
sections.relevance: The warning that it is 'better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into gehenna' is addressed to Jesus's followers, implying that those within the community of disciples face the real possibility of gehenna based on their inner life and conduct. The passage treats the threat of destruction as genuine and avoidable only through radical self-discipline, suggesting that standing before God is not unconditionally guaranteed but requires active vigilance against sin.
key_phrases: it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into gehenna

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage drives past the Deuteronomic provision for divorce to the deeper divine intention for marriage, declaring that divorce (except for sexual immorality) effectively causes adultery because the marriage bond in God's eyes is not severed.
The neutral reading finds this passage prohibits oath-taking entirely, demanding instead a character of radical truthfulness where ordinary speech is inherently trustworthy, making oaths unnecessary.

The neutral reading finds this passage replaces the principle of proportional retaliation with four acts that strip the powerful party of the specific mechanism by which they exercise control -- turning the other cheek forces equal-status engagement, stripping naked in court shames the creditor, the voluntary second mile puts the soldier at risk of violating regulations, and lending without calculating return empties patronage of its binding power -- demonstrating what exceeding righteousness looks like in the face of real powerlessness.

The neutral reading finds this passage commands love of enemies and prayer for persecutors as the climactic demonstration of exceeding righteousness, grounded in resemblance to the Father who provides for evil and good alike, culminating in the demand to 'be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect.'
sections.relevance: The statement that loving enemies is required 'so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven' ties family identity (sonship) to specific conduct. Being recognized as belonging to God's family is presented as contingent on acting like the Father -- specifically, extending indiscriminate love. The implication is that failure to embody this love calls into question one's identity as a child of God. The passage makes the family relationship functionally conditional on conduct that mirrors the Father's character.
key_phrases: so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven
you therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect
if you love those who love you, what reward do you have
